cell.label: Take history and perform complete physical examination, focusing on (but not limited to) affected area, to look for evidence of systemic or other involvement. Obvious etiology of symptoms (e.g., trauma, sprain, strain, fracture)?
Normal activity and physical examination with no worsening symptoms and no constitutional or systemic complaints (e.g., fever, weight loss, rash)?
Underlying illness, immunosuppression, or constitutional complaints (e.g., fever, weight loss, fatigue)?
Consider: Infection (check CBC and ESR), malignancy (check CBC and ESR), and systemic lupus erythematosus (check CBC, ESR, and antinuclear antibodies).
Check CBC and ESR. Consider infection, malignancy, reactive arthritis, and trauma.

Check CBC, ESR and antinuclear antibodies: consider malar, nasal/oral, photosensitive, vasculitic (SLE). Check urinalysis and creatinine: consider Henoch-Schonlein purpura. Consider Erythema marginatum (acute rheumatic fever), Gottron’s papules (juvenile dermatomyositis), and psoriasis (psoriatic arthritis).
Check CBC, ESR, and possible synovial fluid analysis. Consider infection, JRA, reactive arthritis, malignancy, and spondyloarthropathy.
Consider JRA, spondyloarthropathy, SLE, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, and Lyme arthritis.
Reassurance or schedule follow-up if physician or parental concerns exist.

footnotes.footnote: Adapted from Junnila JL, Cartwright VW. Chronic musculoskeletal pain in children: Part I: initial evaluation. Am Fam Phys 2006;74:115–122.
